title: Keeping the Goal
headnote: A boy in the last year of primary school talks about the football game his class plays at break time. He is the one who goes in goal.
text:
I get there first, every break.
You have to, for the jumpers.
Two at their end, two at ours,
paced out with your feet so it's fair,
so nobody argues later when the ball
goes by the post and Kieran swears it was in.

I put myself in goal. Nobody put me there.
Dan does the picking because it's his ball,
and he said, anyone, and I said, me,
and he said, fine, go in.
So that's me choosing.

You can see everything from this end.
That's the bit people don't get.
Up there in the middle you spend the whole game
running at the back of somebody's head.
Back here I know who's tired,
who's got a stitch and won't say it,
who does the same trick every single time,
who looks at the ball too long before he goes.

Fourteen went past me last Tuesday.
I'm not ashamed of fourteen.
Four of them nobody alive could have saved.
One I let in on purpose, because Reece
has never scored in his life,
and you should have seen him after.
I could have had it. I had my hands
on it.

My mum asked if I ever get a go up front.
I told her I don't want one.
She said all right then, love.

Their end has proper netting,
knotted stuff the caretaker put up in March.
Ours is two jumpers and the air between them.
We still say net.
It hit the net. It's in the net.
Nobody has ever once said
there isn't one.

Dan picked me eighth last week. Out of eight.
He was being funny. I laughed as well.

Bell goes. I collect the jumpers,
mine, Reece's, Kieran's, the two blue ones,
and stack them by the fence for tomorrow.
I'm not shifting out of there.
Somebody has to keep the goal.

metadata.form: free verse, unrhymed, no metre, uneven stanza lengths

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: to play in goal, to guard the goal
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: to hold on to something and not give it up
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: The whole ending turns on the two senses sitting in one phrase.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: to stop a shot from going in
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: to rescue someone; to put money aside for later
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: Sits in the same football-and-feeling family as 'keep' and prepares the closing wordplay.
wordVaultCandidates.anchorNote: INFLECTED: the target is 'save' and the text has 'saved'; recorded so no checker has to stem

wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: gathered, as in picked fruit; poked at
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: Repeated with a shift from 'Dan does the picking' to 'Dan picked me eighth', so the word carries the power relationship.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: the upright side of a goal
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: letters delivered to a house; a job or position someone holds
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: The third sense, a position a person is stationed at, is quietly live here.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: a sharp pain in the side from running
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: a loop of thread in sewing
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: Common in playground speech and almost never taught; the sewing sense is the one children know.

wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: light in colour; a funfair; fine weather
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: An everyday word doing thematic work: the boy measures the pitch to be fair and is on the wrong end of something unfair.

wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: changing, as in shifting opinions; a shift of work
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: Colloquial British usage showing register, and its 'changing' sense rubs against a boy who refuses to change his story.

wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: uses rude language; makes a formal promise in court
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: Teaches how context selects a sense, and introduces the theme of claims that may not be true.

contentFlags.issue: Mild social exclusion. The speaker is picked last (eighth out of eight) and is the butt of a joke he joins in with.
contentFlags.reason: Handled without cruelty by the poem itself, entirely ordinary playground experience, and it is the mechanism the whole comprehension task depends on. No adult is unkind and no child is named as a bully; Dan is thoughtless rather than malicious.

contentFlags.issue: A single-parent-shaped detail could be inferred from 'My mum asked', with no father mentioned.
contentFlags.reason: The poem names one parent because that is who asked the question. It assumes nothing about the household and is not commented on.

authoringRead.openingReference: CLEAN. "I get there first, every break" needs nothing before it, and the jumpers are explained in the next three lines. Dan is named at line 8 before he acts, Kieran at 6, Reece at 23.
authoringRead.seams: VACUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION, and answered rather than skipped. A seam is created by joining two spans that were not adjacent in a source. This text has no source and no cuts, so there is no join anywhere in it and the question cannot have a yes. Recorded because an unanswered question and an unaskable one look identical on a passage record.
authoringRead.pronounResolution: VACUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION. The rule fires when a cut removes a paragraph naming a person, leaving the next paragraph's pronouns unresolved. Nothing was cut. Every person in this text is introduced by the text.
authoringRead.itemsLeanOn: NO CLUSTER YET, AND THE STANDING QUESTION IS ANSWERED: TWELVE ITEMS ARE REACHABLE AND SO IS THE USUAL TYPE BALANCE. CORRECTED 2026-08-14: this field first said "about five stated facts a retrieval item could sit on". COUNTED RATHER THAN ESTIMATED THERE ARE NINE — lines 1-6, 8, 9-10, 20-22, 23-25, 28-30, 31-33, 38-39, 40-42. The five was a by-product of reading for affordance and was reported as though it had been measured, which is Addendum 30 exactly. WHAT IS ACTUALLY CONSTRAINED IS LINE-SPACE, NOT FACT SUPPLY. 44 lines; the two-span T4 takes 7-11 and 38-39 and the whole-text takes none, leaving ten windows across about 39 lines — 3.9 lines each, and verse lines are shorter than prose, so nearer 25 words per window. The cost is windows small enough that a stem names two or three lines, with CHECK 1 binding on almost every pair. The failure mode at that size is a distractor that cannot be defeated from inside its own window, which is cold-read Q5 and not a gate. If an item cannot defeat its distractors in three lines, ship eleven with the shortfall stated rather than a twelfth built on a fact that will not carry three wrong options.

The key — that he could have stopped it and chose not to — needs line 23 to establish that he let it in on purpose, and line 23 sits outside the window. That is cold-read Q5, and verify_clusters passed the item without comment because span sufficiency is a reader's question and not a gate. Merged into one item on 23-27.
